data.name: Time Tenshi (2015)
data.detailed_description:
The Time Window...



An incredible invention, developed over decades in secret, empowers humans to make their grandest dream a reality...

To travel through time!

At a hidden research facility, Rose and Kyo - the Time Tenshi (Time Angels) - voyage into the past in secret under the watchful eye of Tensai Shiro, the mastermind behind the Time Window, and Michelle, the base's Commander and Operations Manager.

Since time travel is still dangerous and experimental, the Time Window has yet to be tested on male subjects, meaning only females can safely venture back into history. They seem to undergo some surprising changes to their bodies in certain areas while doing so...

But a sinister organisation called Chrontek found a way to hack into Shiro's machine, and now Chrontek is pursuing its own devious plans for the flow of time...

Can time travel be entrusted to humans?

What happens when the Time Window goes wrong?

And can the Time Tenshi stop the girls of Chrontek... before history is changed forever?

-- -- --

Time Tenshi is an exciting anime/ecchi visual novel! As the player's character enters Tensai Shiro's lab facility and follows the Time Tenshi in their journeys through time, a plot full of futuristic action, ecchi, humour and plenty of fanservice will unfold!

reviews.review:
Time Tenshi (2015) takes the familiar visual novel format and builds it around an entertaining mixture of time travel, anime comedy, science fiction, and unapologetic ecchi fanservice. Developed and published by Silver Cow Studio, it presents an imaginative premise without pretending to be a complicated simulation of temporal mechanics. Instead, the concept of traveling into the past provides the framework for a character-focused adventure that alternates between potentially serious threats to history and intentionally provocative humor.

The story centers on the Time Window, an experimental invention created after years of secret research. Rose and Kyo serve as the Time Angels who use the machine to travel into the past, while inventor Tensai Shiro and operations manager Michelle supervise their activities from a concealed research facility. The technology is still considered dangerous, and the unusual restriction that only women can safely use it becomes both a plot element and an excuse for some of the story's more exaggerated fanservice. The premise is deliberately absurd in places, but it fits the playful tone the narrative establishes.

A more substantial conflict arrives through Chrontek, an organization that discovers a way to interfere with the Time Window. Rather than treating time travel merely as an opportunity for sightseeing, the plot introduces the possibility that history itself could be manipulated for selfish purposes. This gives the narrative some welcome urgency and raises interesting questions about whether people should possess the ability to rewrite events in the first place. The potential consequences of malfunctioning technology and deliberate historical interference give the adventure a stronger foundation than its fanservice-heavy presentation initially suggests.

Despite these science-fiction ideas, the experience remains fundamentally an anime and ecchi visual novel. Reading dialogue and following story sequences constitute the majority of the gameplay, so anyone expecting extensive exploration, puzzles, combat, or sophisticated manipulation of timelines may be disappointed. Its strengths instead depend on the personalities of its cast, comedic exchanges, artwork, and the gradual development of the conflict. The relatively passive structure works adequately for players who enjoy straightforward visual novels, although greater interaction could have made the time-travel premise significantly more engaging.

The characters carry much of the experience. Rose and Kyo naturally occupy central positions because they directly participate in the journeys through history, while Shiro's role as the inventor gives him responsibility for a technology capable of producing enormous consequences. Michelle provides another important presence within the laboratory, while Chrontek gives the protagonists a recognizable enemy. The characterization tends toward colorful anime archetypes rather than subtle psychological development, but that approach suits the game's deliberately heightened personality.

Visually, the presentation is designed around anime-style character artwork and suggestive imagery. Fanservice is not an incidental element but one of the primary attractions, with the Steam description explicitly emphasizing ecchi material, humor, and mature themes. Some nudity and sexual content are also identified by the store. Consequently, the game is best approached by an adult audience already comfortable with this particular style. Players interested in the science-fiction concept but uncomfortable with sexualized anime material are unlikely to find the presentation appealing.

One of its greatest missed opportunities is the limited exploration of cause and effect. A story about traveling through history naturally creates expectations of branching timelines, difficult choices, paradoxes, and dramatically different outcomes. Here, those possibilities primarily support the predetermined narrative rather than becoming elaborate interactive systems. The player generally follows the unfolding adventure instead of personally shaping history. This makes the experience approachable, but it also prevents the concept from reaching the depth it potentially could have achieved.

The contrast between serious science-fiction questions and deliberately silly fanservice is simultaneously a strength and weakness. There are legitimate ideas concerning technological responsibility, interference with history, and the consequences of allowing powerful inventions to fall into hostile hands. Yet the story rarely abandons its lighthearted identity long enough to examine those subjects deeply. Players looking for rigorous time-travel fiction may therefore find it superficial, while those interested in a humorous anime adventure are more likely to appreciate the balance.

Its overall presentation is modest, but the smaller production scale suits a visual novel that concentrates primarily on dialogue, character illustrations, and narrative progression. English interface and subtitles are supported, while full voice acting is not listed. Steam also identifies it as a single-player experience with Trading Cards and Family Sharing. These features do little to transform the fundamental experience, but they reinforce its straightforward nature.

Steam Deck compatibility deserves some qualification. Steam does not currently display an official Valve Steam Deck compatibility rating for the title. However, the game has Linux support listed and is built using technology associated with Ren'Py/Python, which generally makes this type of visual novel less demanding than conventional 3D games. Steam's review interface also recognizes Steam Deck playtime filtering for the game. Still, without an official Verified or Playable designation, Deck owners should regard compatibility as unofficial rather than guaranteed. The visual-novel structure itself is naturally suited to handheld play if it runs correctly.

Overall, this is a niche visual novel that knows the audience it wants to entertain. Its combination of time travel, anime characters, comedy, mature material, and a villainous organization attempting to manipulate history gives it more narrative identity than a basic fanservice title. The limited interactivity and relatively shallow treatment of its most interesting science-fiction concepts hold it back, but its eccentric personality provides a certain charm. Those seeking sophisticated temporal storytelling will probably want something deeper, whereas fans of lighthearted ecchi visual novels may find its unusual premise entertaining.

Rating: 7/10
